newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Labor strike threat recedes in South Korea.
newsitem.headline: Labor strike threat recedes in South Korea.

text.p: Militant South Korean unionists called off a strike threatened for Friday in protest at planned labour law changes, and the government hinted it may be unable to force the measures through this year.

The immediate threat to South Korea's export industry receded after the outlawed Korea Confederation of Trade Unions postponed a scheduled four-hour walkout by its 500,000 members in 300 companies, including Hyundai Motor Co and Daewoo Heavy Industries Co.
But the unions made clear they could strike at any time unless the ruling New Korea Party scrapped legal revisions permitting layoffs and flexible work hours.

The country's largest labour union umbrella group, the Federation of Korean Trade Unions, said it would go ahead with stoppages planned for Monday and Thursday next week unless the government backed down.

Parliament adjourns on December 18, and the ruling New Korea Party still wants the labour bill passed "if not during this session, then in an extraordinary session before the end of the year", said party official Kim Jong-man.
But Kim, a policy adviser on labour and environmental affairs, suggested that may not be possible.
The ruling party "feels a need to discuss the matter with the opposition before the bill is passed, and I don't think at the moment the other parties will accept the call for a debate," he said.
Opposition parties have united to demand a delay.

"We cannot pass the bill as it is now because issues like worker layoffs, flexible working hours and replacement of striking workers are difficult to accept," said Bang Yong-seok, a member of parliament for the main opposition National Congress for New Politics.
"If the ruling party tries to forcibly ram the bill through, strikes by workers will be inevitable," he said.

Yoon Young-mo, a spokesman for the outlawed union organisation, said Friday's stoppage was put off because it was unlikely the changes would be pushed through this year, but strikes were still an option.
"Leaders of our member unions have been told to remain in close contact with the confederation so all our member workers can go on a strike at any time," Yoon said.
Choi Dae-yul, an official at the press office of the Federation of Korean Trade Unions, said: "There are no changes to our plans".
"It depends on the labour law," he said. "If they don't cancel the changes, we will go ahead with our strikes."
The federation, which represents 1.2 million workers at 800 companies, plans a one-hour stoppage on Monday and a three-hour walkout on Thursday.

The New Korea Party appealed to the union bodies on Thursday to drop plans for industrial action, saying it was "sympathetic" to labour but it was impossible to change the law and satisfy both workers and managers.

Employer groups object to the first revisions to restrictive labour legislation in 43 years that would allow mulitiple unions in each workplace, a move they say would lead to greater militancy as labour unions vied for members.
South Korea was spurred to revise its labour laws by membership of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development. It formally joined the Paris-based club of rich nations on Thursday.
